ONE CLAIM. HUNDREDS OF SEARCHES.

You advocate for policyholders.{{tw4Text}}. You don't write blog posts. You don't have to.

Every event in the life of a claim automatically becomes a searchable article Google can index.

Not because CLAIMtract writes content.
Because every claim event contains questions homeowners are already asking.

  • A roof inspection becomes answers about leaks, stains, and storm damage.
  • A mold assessment becomes answers about water intrusion and microbial growth.
  • A carrier estimate becomes answers about underpayments, missed damage, and claim disputes.

As you update the file, CLAIMtract analyzes each note, finding, photo, document, and expert opinion, then maps that information to real homeowner search behavior. Every update strengthens the core case study while expanding a growing network of Cluster Articles designed around the problems homeowners are actively searching for.

You keep documenting the claim.
CLAIMtract turns that documentation into syndicated search authority.

EVERY EVENT. EVERY UPDATE. EVERY FINDING.

If your claim file already contains the answers homeowners are searching for, why should those answers stay hidden inside your head?

ROOF · WIND DAMAGE
Found Shingles in Your Yard After a Storm? Here's What It Means for Your Roof.
JQJohn Q. Adjuster · Public adjuster

Most homeowners see shingles in the yard and assume they just need a small repair. What they don't realize is those shingles were the first layer protecting the home from water.

"The missing shingle isn't the claim. It's the beginning of the claim."

Creased shingles are often evidence that wind broke the seal. Left alone, water may not show up inside until the next heavy rain.

Here's what to photograph before you call anyone, and what to ask your insurance company.

PILLAR ARTICLE · CASE STUDY

Wind Damage

{{synPlace}}
By John Q. Adjuster, Licensed Public Adjuster

Wind damage is rarely just about wind damage. A lifted shingle can lead to questions about coverage, inspections, moisture intrusion, claim documentation, roof replacement thresholds, and carrier evaluations. To address those questions comprehensively, every Pillar Article begins with a 2,000+ word case study sourced from an actual claim. That case study then becomes the foundation for a growing network of supporting articles, FAQs, local resources, and homeowner answers. Each page is cross-linked, schema-enhanced, and structured to reinforce the others, creating a Wikipedia-style authority framework that demonstrates real-world experience while helping search engines understand topical depth and relevance.

Instead of publishing a single article, ClaimTract transforms one claim into a compounding authority asset built to strengthen visibility over time.

A few lifted shingles after a storm don't look like much from the driveway. But wind that lifts a shingle can also break the seal underneath, and water finds that gap long before a stain shows on the ceiling. That's why the first inspection matters: what gets photographed and written down now is what the carrier weighs later.

07 · WHO BUILT THIS

I'm not a software company. I'm a former Florida-licensed public insurance adjuster, author, and software architect who wrote more claims as an individual than most firms.

For 17 years I worked Florida claims. Tyvek suits in flea-infested houses, respirators in mold jobs, roofs, attics, crawl spaces. I wrote 30 to 50 houses a month, about three claims a house. Some months I had 54 files on my desk, by myself.

I didn't live on referrals. Before I wrote my first contract, I had 30 computers running in my garage generating leads. That's the part nobody teaches you.

The carriers noticed. Every file with my name on it went straight to an examination under oath, and some days I sat through two.

Eventually I retired, moved to Thailand, and traveled. But I couldn't stop thinking about the business. That thinking turned into four books. Two are published on Amazon, and both are the foundation this app is built on.

When you use ClaimTract, you're not talking to a support desk. You're talking to me.
